The activation peaks at the boundary where the call's continuation is defined (e.g., ').' before .success(function(', 'String.class' for AjaxCallback, 'click(function('), or on security-related parameters like password. The firing is retrospective: it reads ahead through the call's arguments to recognize the callback/event handler pattern (AjaxCallback class name, .success() method name, .click() event handler), then fires at the marker where the continuation is registered. Examples driven mostly by surrounding context (http.post string, url parameter) because they show the callback pattern clearly; examples driven mostly by the peak token (click, password) because those tokens themselves signal the callback/event or security context.

Q: AndroidQuery ajax doesn't call php page when page contains IFRAME I tried the following code to access my PHP page: String url = "http://mypage.example.com/test.php?name="+data; aq.ajax(url, String.class, new AjaxCallback() { @Override public void callback(String url, String html, AjaxStatus status) { Log.w(Tags.DEBUG,String.valueOf(status.getCode())); } }); My PHP page writes a file if the call was made. When I use the URL inside a browser, the file is created. When I use my Android app, nothing happens, the status code is 200. What else should I set? UPDATE: The source of my page: MY WEBSITE <body bgcolor=#FFFFFF text=#000000> <a href="http://example.com/user12/test.php">http://example.com/user12/test.php</a> </body> A: It seems that the web page was the problem, it sent back its source code and there was an IFRAME in it.

Q:

ssh authentication failure with public/private keys

I'm setting up a Continuous Deployment pipeline on gitlab.
Unfortunately, when trying to ssh from the pipeline to the target server, the authentication fails.
I am asking the question here because I am fairly sure the problem is unix related and not gitlab.
Here is the setup:

Using ssh-keygen I created a key pair.
I added the public key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server.
The private key is export in an env var 'SSH_PRIVATE_KEY' on the client server.
permissions on the server: ~/.ssh 700, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys 600
sshd configs on the server are all defaults.

On commit, gitlab spins up a docker executor (docker image node:11.2).
Then, those commands are executed inside the container:
'which ssh-agent || ( apt-get update -y && apt-get install openssh-client -y )'
eval $(ssh-agent -s)

    ##
    ## Add the SSH key stored in SSH_PRIVATE_KEY variable to the agent store
    ## We're using tr to fix line endings which makes ed25519 keys work
    ## without extra base64 encoding.
    ## https://gitlab.com/gitlab-examples/ssh-private-key/issues/1#note_48526556
    ##
echo "$SSH_PRIVATE_KEY" | tr -d '\r' | ssh-add - > /dev/null

mkdir -p ~/.ssh
chmod 700 ~/.ssh

echo "$SSH_PRIVATE_KEY" > ~/.ssh/known_hosts
chmod 644 ~/.ssh/known_hosts
ssh -vvv user@server

I followed the instructions here: https://docs.gitlab.com/ce/ci/ssh_keys/

A:

Giving a POC-like answer which is using an ugly loop and not the most beatiful design:
Loading eg. the xlxs package to be able to write to Excel 2007 format:
library(xlsx)

Let us create a workbook and a sheet (see the manual!):
wb <- createWorkbook()
sheet <- createSheet(wb, "demo")

Define some styles to use in the spreadsheet:
red <- createCellStyle(wb, fillBackgroundColor="tomato", fillForegroundColor="yellow", fillPattern="BIG_SPOTS")
yellow <- createCellStyle(wb, fillBackgroundColor="yellow", fillForegroundColor="tomato", fillPattern="BRICKS1")

And the ugly loop which is pasting each cell to the spreadsheet with appropriate format:
for (i in 1:nrow(pval)) {
    rows <- createRow(sheet, rowIndex=i)
    for (j in 1:ncol(pval)) {
        cell.1 <- createCell(rows, colIndex=j)[[1,1]]
        setCellValue(cell.1, gen[i,j])
        if ((pval[i,j] < 0.3) | (pval[i,j] > 0.7)) {
            setCellStyle(cell.1, red)
        } else {
            setCellStyle(cell.1, yellow)
        }
    }
}

Saving the Excel file:
saveWorkbook(wb, '/tmp/demo.xls')

Result: demo.xls

adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative targeting token identity shortcut. The peak token 'success' appears here without any callback context, function registration, or async continuation pattern.
Hard negative targeting punctuation shortcut. Contains 'password' token and the exact string '.success(' pattern, but it's a condition check (if statement), not a callback/event handler registration.
Hard negative targeting 'any function' shortcut. Contains the peak token 'success' as a function name in the body of a regular function call, not as part of a callback registration pattern.

Hard negative targeting 'any callback' shortcut. Contains 'click' token and callback syntax, but this is an event listener attached directly to an element, not a jQuery-style callback registration with a marker token.

Hard negative targeting token identity and syntax shortcut. Contains 'String.class' and 'callback' as separate tokens with a generic space-separated pattern, but no actual function call, continuation marker, or callback registration.

Hard negative targeting token identity shortcut. Uses 'onSuccess' variable naming and function syntax similar to the hypothesis, but this is a standalone function assignment without any call to register the callback, no callback/event context.

Hard negative targeting 'any call expression' shortcut. Contains '.success(' as an option property, not a method call marker or continuation point. The hypothesis relies on the '.success(' being at a specific boundary in a call expression.

Hard negative targeting language/framework mismatch. Uses JavaScript Promise pattern with .then() instead of .success(), but still represents an async continuation point. Tests if the hypothesis is overly specific to the callback/event handler patterns shown in examples.
Hard negative targeting function name shortcut. Contains 'callback' as a standalone function definition, not as part of a callback registration or continuation pattern.

Hard negative targeting HTTP/URL context shortcut. Contains 'POST' and 'endpoint' but no callback, event handler, or continuation marker. Tests if the hypothesis is over-indexing on HTTP/URL patterns from examples.

Positive holdout testing offshoot variant. Similar to Node.js stream handlers but with a success event instead of data. If the hypothesis commits to event handler patterns broadly, this should activate.
